newsitem.title: JAPAN: Greying Japan must change labour law -- panel member.
newsitem.headline: Greying Japan must change labour law -- panel member.

text.p: Unless Japan overhauls its employment laws immediately to cope with the country's rapidly ageing population "it will be suicidal", a key member of a labour reform panel said on Thursday.

Haruo Shimada, head of a subcommittee of the Economic Council, an advisory panel to the prime minister, told reporters that while the number of workers would fall rapidly after 2010, Japan still had employment laws established half a century ago.
"If we don't start (reform and deregulation) immediately, it will be suicidal," said Shimada, a professor at Keio University in Tokyo.

To cope with increased costs stemming from the greying of society, and a falling number of people in the labour market, Japan must pass measures to make more effective use of its workers, Shimada said.
The Health and Welfare Ministry has estimated that people aged 65 and over will account for 21.9 percent of Japan's population in 2010 and 27.4 percent in 2025, up from 14.8 percent in 1995.
But those of working age, between 20 and 64, will fall to 56.7 percent of the population in 2025, down from 59.3 percent in 2010 and 62.4 percent last year.
Japan's current population is about 125.6 million.
The subcommittee on deregulation, set up in July by the Economic Planning Agency (EPA), is made up of leading figures from the private sector and academics.

The subcommittee's proposal, which was presented to the advisory panel on Thursday, will be used as an outline for the panel's final recommendation to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in December, an EPA official said.
The proposal called for easing regulations on job placement and temporary staff businesses to make it easier for people to enter the labour market.
For example, it said a tax law which encouraged housewives to stay away from the full-time work market should be dropped.
